final_answer: This is my analysis. Antibiotic resistance arises through natural selection, an evolutionary mechanism where bacteria with genetic mutations that confer resistance to antibiotics survive and reproduce more successfully than non-resistant strains. When antibiotics are used, they kill susceptible bacteria, but resistant bacteria, which may have acquired resistance through mutations or horizontal gene transfer (e.g., plasmid exchange), survive. Over time, these resistant strains become more prevalent in the population. Overprescription accelerates this process by exposing bacteria to antibiotics unnecessarily or in suboptimal doses, which allows resistant strains to thrive while killing off non-resistant competitors. This selective pressure favors resistance, leading to the rapid emergence and spread of drug-resistant pathogens. Additionally, misuse (e.g., incomplete courses) can leave behind partially resistant bacteria, further driving resistance. This undermines the effectiveness of antibiotics, making infections harder to treat and increasing public health risks. This is my analysis.
